mainEntity.name: What is an abstract class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An abstract class in Java is a class declared with the 'abstract' keyword that cannot be instantiated directly — you cannot create an object of an abstract class using 'new'. It serves as a partially implemented base class that defines a common contract (via abstract methods) and optionally provides shared implementation (via concrete methods, fields, and constructors). Abstract classes are designed to be extended by concrete subclasses, which must provide implementations for all inherited abstract methods. They represent the concept of incomplete design — defining WHAT subclasses must do without specifying HOW they do it.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between abstract class and interface in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Abstract class: can have instance variables (state), constructors, concrete methods, abstract methods; supports single inheritance; use when subclasses share common state or behavior. Interface: no instance variables (only public static final constants before Java 8; default/static methods from Java 8+); no constructors; supports multiple inheritance; use when unrelated classes need to fulfill a common contract. Rule of thumb: use abstract class for IS-A relationships with shared state/behavior (Vehicle → Car); use interface for CAN-DO capabilities across unrelated hierarchies (Serializable, Comparable, Runnable).

mainEntity.name: Can an abstract class have a constructor in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Abstract classes can and often do have constructors, even though abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly. The constructor of an abstract class is called by subclass constructors via the 'super()' call. It is used to initialize fields declared in the abstract class. If you do not define a constructor in the abstract class, Java provides a default no-arg constructor. Abstract class constructors cannot be called with 'new AbstractClass()' — they are only invoked through super() chains from concrete subclasses.

mainEntity.name: What is an abstract method in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An abstract method is a method declared with the 'abstract' keyword that has NO method body — only a signature and semicolon: 'public abstract double calculateArea();'. It defines a contract that every non-abstract subclass MUST implement. Rules: (1) Abstract methods can only exist in abstract classes or interfaces. (2) A non-abstract (concrete) subclass MUST implement all inherited abstract methods — failing to do so causes a compile error. (3) Abstract methods cannot be private (a private method cannot be overridden by subclasses). (4) Abstract methods cannot be static (static methods belong to the class, not to polymorphic dispatch). (5) Abstract methods cannot be final (final prevents overriding, which contradicts the purpose of abstract).

mainEntity.name: What is a concrete class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A concrete class is any class that provides complete implementations for all its methods — including all inherited abstract methods — and can be directly instantiated with 'new'. It is the opposite of an abstract class. A concrete class may extend an abstract class (implementing all abstract methods) or implement an interface (providing all interface method bodies). Most ordinary Java classes are concrete classes. If a class extends an abstract class but does not implement all abstract methods, it must itself be declared abstract.

blocks.text: Abstraction is one of the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming. It is the principle of hiding implementation complexity and exposing only the essential interface to the outside world. Abstraction answers the question: "What does this thing do?" — while hiding "How does it do it?".

Real-world analogy: when you drive a car, you interact with the steering wheel, accelerator, and brakes — the abstract interface. You do not need to understand the internal combustion engine, gear transmission, or anti-lock braking system underneath. The car exposes WHAT you can do (steer, accelerate, brake), not HOW it works internally. Java implements abstraction through two mechanisms: abstract classes and interfaces.

blocks.title: 🔑 Two Mechanisms of Abstraction in Java
blocks.text: Java provides abstraction through: (1) Abstract classes — partial abstraction; can have both abstract methods (contract) and concrete methods (shared implementation). Use when subclasses share state or common behavior. (2) Interfaces — full abstraction (pre-Java 8); a pure contract with no implementation. Use when unrelated classes need to fulfill a common capability. This chapter covers abstract classes and concrete classes in depth. Interfaces are covered in the next chapter.

sections.title: What is an Abstract Class in Java?

blocks.text: An abstract class in Java is a class declared with the abstract keyword. It represents an incomplete design — it may define some behavior (concrete methods, fields, constructors) but leaves certain behaviors undefined (abstract methods) for subclasses to provide. Because it is incomplete, an abstract class cannot be instantiated directly. It exists solely to be extended.

Abstract classes are the ideal tool when you have a family of related classes that share common state and behavior, but differ in specific operations. For example: Shape is abstract — all shapes have a color and a position (shared state), and all shapes can be drawn (shared behavior), but the specific calculation of area differs per shape type. Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle are concrete subclasses that implement calculateArea() in their own way.

items.title: Syntax
What It Can Contain
items.text:
1. Instance variables (fields) — shared state for all subclasses.
2. Constructors — initialized via super() from subclasses.
3. Concrete (non-abstract) methods — shared behavior.
4. Abstract methods — contract that subclasses MUST implement.
5. Static methods and static variables — fully supported.
6. final methods — shared behavior that CANNOT be overridden.

items.title: How It Works
items.text: Abstract class defined → Extended by concrete subclass → Subclass MUST implement all abstract methods → Concrete subclass can be instantiated → Objects accessed through abstract class reference for polymorphism.

sections.title: What is a Concrete Class in Java?

blocks.text: A concrete class is any class that provides complete implementations for all its methods — including all abstract methods inherited from any abstract parent class or interface — and can therefore be directly instantiated with new. Every ordinary Java class you have written so far is a concrete class. The word 'concrete' implies completeness: nothing is left undefined.

blocks.title: 💡 Concrete Class = Instantiable + Complete
blocks.text: The two defining properties of a concrete class: (1) It is NOT declared abstract. (2) It provides implementations for ALL abstract methods — either directly, or by inheriting them from a non-abstract parent. If a subclass extends an abstract class but does not implement all abstract methods, it MUST itself be declared abstract — it becomes a partial (abstract) subclass, not a concrete one.

An abstract method is a method declared with the abstract keyword that has no body — just a signature terminated by a semicolon. It defines a contract: every non-abstract subclass must provide its own implementation. Abstract methods are the mechanism through which abstract classes enforce a common API across all concrete subclasses.

items.title: Valid Abstract Method Modifiers
Invalid Abstract Method Modifiers
items.text:

static abstract void method();   // ❌ static doesn't participate in polymorphism

native abstract void method();   // ❌ native implies a body exists
synchronized abstract void m();  // ❌ synchronized implies a body

items.title: Abstract Method Rules
items.text:
1. Can ONLY exist in an abstract class or interface.
2. Has NO body — only signature + semicolon.
3. Every concrete (non-abstract) subclass MUST implement it.
4. If a subclass doesn't implement it, the subclass must be declared abstract.
5. The implementing method in subclass must use @Override.
6. An abstract class can have ZERO abstract methods (valid but unusual).

sections.title: Rules of Abstract Classes — The Complete Ruleset

blocks.text: The Java compiler enforces strict rules for abstract classes. Understanding every rule prevents unexpected compile errors and design mistakes.

items.title: Rule 1 — Cannot Be Instantiated
items.text: An abstract class CANNOT be instantiated with 'new'. new AbstractClass() is always a compile error. However, an abstract class CAN be used as a reference type for polymorphism: AbstractClass ref = new ConcreteSubclass().

items.title: Rule 2 — Subclass Must Implement All Abstract Methods
items.text: A concrete (non-abstract) subclass that extends an abstract class MUST provide implementations for ALL abstract methods inherited from the parent. Missing even one abstract method implementation → compile error unless the subclass is also declared abstract.

items.title: Rule 3 — Abstract Class CAN Have Zero Abstract Methods
items.text: An abstract class is not required to contain any abstract methods — it just needs the 'abstract' keyword on the class declaration. This is valid and useful when you want to prevent direct instantiation of a class while still providing full implementation. Example: a utility base class not intended for direct use.

items.title: Rule 4 — Abstract Class CAN Have Constructors
items.text: Abstract classes can define constructors. These are not called directly (you cannot new AbstractClass()), but they ARE invoked through super() calls from subclass constructors. They initialize the shared fields declared in the abstract class.

items.title: Rule 5 — Abstract Class CAN Have Concrete Methods
items.text: Abstract classes can freely mix abstract and concrete methods. Concrete methods provide shared implementation available to all subclasses. This is the key advantage over interfaces (pre-Java 8) — abstract classes can hold real, shared logic.

items.title: Rule 6 — Abstract Class CAN Have Static & Final Members
items.text: Static methods, static variables, and final methods are all allowed in abstract classes. final methods are inherited but CANNOT be overridden — useful for enforcing invariant behavior across the hierarchy. Static methods belong to the class itself and are not subject to overriding.

items.title: Rule 7 — Abstract Class Supports Single Inheritance Only
items.text: A class can extend only ONE abstract class (Java's single inheritance rule). To achieve multiple type inheritance, use interfaces. A class can extend one abstract class AND implement multiple interfaces simultaneously.

items.title: Rule 8 — Abstract Class Can Extend Another Abstract Class
items.text: An abstract class can extend another abstract class without implementing its abstract methods — it passes the obligation down to the first concrete subclass. This enables multi-level abstract hierarchies where each level adds new abstract contracts.

blocks.text: Abstract classes can have constructors — and they frequently should. Even though an abstract class cannot be instantiated directly, its constructor is called every time a concrete subclass is instantiated, via the super() call in the subclass constructor. Abstract class constructors serve the essential role of initializing the shared fields defined in the abstract class, ensuring every subclass object starts with a valid base state.

blocks.title: 📌 Constructor Chaining in Abstract Hierarchies
blocks.text: When a concrete subclass is instantiated, Java calls constructors from top to bottom in the hierarchy — the most abstract ancestor first, the concrete class last. If a subclass constructor does not explicitly call super(...), Java inserts a no-arg super() call automatically. If the abstract class has no no-arg constructor (only parameterized ones), the subclass MUST explicitly call super(args) — otherwise a compile error occurs.

sections.title: Extending an Abstract Class — The Full Pattern

blocks.text: Extending an abstract class follows the same syntax as extending any class — class ConcreteClass extends AbstractClass. The key obligation: the concrete subclass must implement every abstract method it inherits. Each implementation should use @Override for compiler validation. The subclass also inherits all concrete methods and fields from the abstract parent.

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface — When to Use Which

blocks.text: Choosing between an abstract class and an interface is one of the most important OOP design decisions in Java. Both provide abstraction, but they serve different purposes and impose different constraints. With Java 8+ default methods, the boundary has narrowed, but the fundamental distinction remains: abstract class = IS-A relationship with shared state; interface = CAN-DO capability.

✅ Yes — freely mix concrete and abstract

blocks.title: 💡 The Golden Rule for Abstract Class vs Interface
blocks.text: Ask two questions: (1) Do the related classes share COMMON STATE (fields)? → Abstract class. (2) Are unrelated classes (from different hierarchies) sharing the SAME CAPABILITY? → Interface. In practice: use abstract class when building a class family (Vehicle hierarchy, Shape hierarchy); use interface when defining cross-cutting capabilities (Serializable, Comparable, Printable, Auditable). You can — and often should — use both together: class ConcreteClass extends AbstractBase implements Interface1, Interface2.

sections.title: Template Method Pattern — The Classic Abstract Class Design Pattern

blocks.text: The Template Method Pattern is the most natural design pattern for abstract classes. It defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a concrete method of the abstract class, deferring specific steps to abstract methods that subclasses implement. The abstract class controls the sequence of steps; the subclasses provide the implementation of individual steps. The template method itself is often declared final to prevent subclasses from altering the algorithm structure.

blocks.label: TemplateMethodPattern.java
lines: * Template Method Pattern — Data Import Pipeline
* Abstract class defines the fixed sequence (validate → parse → transform → save).
// ✅ TEMPLATE METHOD — final so subclasses cannot change the algorithm flow
// Step 4: Transform — optional hook (has default no-op implementation)
// Hook method — optional override; default is a no-op
// Concrete step — shared by all importers
System.out.println("✅ Saved " + records.length + " records to database");
return rawData.split("\n"); // Simple line split for demo
// Concrete subclass — JSON Importer (overrides hook method too)
// ✅ Overrides hook method — adds transformation step

blocks.title: 💡 Hook Methods — Optional Extension Points
blocks.text: A hook method is a concrete method in the abstract class with a default (often empty) implementation that subclasses MAY override to add behavior at a specific point in the algorithm. Unlike abstract methods (which subclasses MUST implement), hook methods are optional extension points. In the example above, 'transform()' is a hook — CSVImporter accepts the default no-op, while JSONImporter adds its own normalization logic. Hooks make the Template Method Pattern flexible without forcing every subclass to implement every step.

blocks.text: These mistakes appear consistently in beginner and intermediate Java code involving abstract classes. Most compile without obvious errors but lead to incorrect design or subtle runtime behavior.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns involving abstract classes are common causes of failed code reviews and brittle class hierarchies in professional Java teams.

items.title: Abstract Class with No Abstract Methods
items.text: Declaring a class abstract just to prevent instantiation, when no abstract methods exist, is a code smell. If the reason is 'this class should not be used directly', consider making the constructor package-private or protected instead. An abstract class with zero abstract methods provides no polymorphic contract — it is an abuse of the mechanism. The only valid exception: deliberate use of the Template Method pattern where hook methods are all concrete.

items.title: Deep Abstract Hierarchy (Inheritance Hell)
items.text: Chains of abstract classes 5–6 levels deep become impossible to trace and maintain. Each new level adds cognitive overhead for every developer who reads the code. Prefer COMPOSITION over INHERITANCE for code reuse beyond 2–3 levels. Deep hierarchies violate the principle that subclasses should be understandable without reading all their ancestors.

items.title: Fat Abstract Class (Doing Too Much)
items.text: An abstract class that mixes unrelated responsibilities — logging, validation, persistence, and business logic all in one — becomes a god class. Every subclass inherits all of this bloat, even if it only needs one piece. Prefer small, focused abstract classes. Move unrelated concerns to interfaces or injected collaborators (composition).

items.title: Overriding Concrete Methods Without Good Reason
items.text: Concrete methods in an abstract class represent guaranteed shared behavior. If subclasses routinely override them with completely different logic, the shared method serves no real purpose. This is a sign the hierarchy is wrong — the shared behavior isn't actually shared. Reconsider whether these classes truly belong in the same hierarchy.

items.title: Exposing Abstract Class Constructor as Public
items.text: The constructor of an abstract class can never be called directly (abstract classes cannot be instantiated). Making it public misleads readers into thinking it can be. Abstract class constructors should be protected — only subclass constructors in the same or different packages need to call super(). A public constructor on an abstract class is never needed.

items.title: Using Abstract Class Where Interface Suffices
items.text: If your abstract class has no instance fields and no concrete methods (pure abstract methods only), replace it with an interface. Interfaces support multiple inheritance, are more flexible, and impose less coupling. This is the most common misuse — using abstract class as a 'poor man's interface' when a real interface would be better.

blocks.label: AbstractAntiPatterns.java
lines: // ❌ ANTI-PATTERN 1: Abstract class used as pure interface — no fields, no concrete methods
// ❌ ANTI-PATTERN 2: Public constructor on abstract class
abstract class A { abstract void doA(); }
abstract class B extends A { abstract void doB(); }
abstract class C extends B { abstract void doC(); }
abstract class D extends C { abstract void doD(); }
// Must implement doA, doB, doC, doD — impossible to read without tracing 4 levels
void doA() {} void doB() {} void doC() {} void doD() {}
// ✅ BETTER: Flatten with interfaces + one abstract class + composition

sections.title: Java Abstract Class Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced developer interviews, OCPJP certification exams, and campus placement tests.

items.q: Q1. What is an abstract class in Java? Why can't it be instantiated?
items.a: An abstract class is a class declared with the 'abstract' keyword that represents an incomplete design. It may contain abstract methods (no body — just a contract) and concrete methods (full implementation). It cannot be instantiated because it may have unimplemented (abstract) methods — calling them on a direct instance would be undefined behavior since there is no implementation. The purpose is to serve as a base class: subclasses provide the missing implementations and CAN be instantiated. Even if an abstract class has zero abstract methods, 'abstract' on the class declaration itself prevents direct instantiation by design choice.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
items.a: Abstract class: can have instance variables (state), constructors, both abstract and concrete methods; supports only single inheritance. Interface: no instance variables (only constants), no constructors, methods are implicitly public and abstract (except Java 8+ default/static methods); supports multiple inheritance. Use abstract class for IS-A relationships among related classes that share state and behavior (Vehicle → Car). Use interface for CAN-DO capabilities across unrelated hierarchies (Runnable, Serializable, Comparable). A class can extend ONE abstract class but implement MANY interfaces. Since Java 8 blurred the line with default methods, the key remaining distinction is: abstract class can hold shared mutable state; interface cannot.

items.q: Q3. Can an abstract class have a constructor? If yes, how is it called?
items.a: Yes. Abstract classes can and should have constructors for initializing their shared fields. The constructor cannot be called via 'new AbstractClass()' (compile error) but IS called through the super() chain when a concrete subclass is instantiated. Every subclass constructor implicitly or explicitly calls super() — this triggers the abstract class constructor. If the abstract class has only parameterized constructors (no default), the subclass MUST call super(args) explicitly, or a compile error occurs. Abstract class constructors should be protected (not public) since they are never called directly.

items.q: Q4. Can an abstract class have concrete (non-abstract) methods?
items.a: Yes — absolutely. Abstract classes can freely mix abstract and concrete methods. Concrete methods in abstract classes provide SHARED behavior that all subclasses inherit and can use without re-implementing. This is the primary advantage over interfaces (which pre-Java 8 had no concrete methods at all). Examples: a Shape abstract class might have a concrete display() method (same for all shapes) alongside abstract calculateArea() and calculatePerimeter() (different per shape). This is the Template Method Pattern — the abstract class owns the overall behavior structure, subclasses fill in the varying parts.

items.q: Q5. Can an abstract class exist without any abstract methods?
items.a: Yes. A class with zero abstract methods can still be declared abstract — this simply prevents direct instantiation. This is a valid design choice when: (1) You want to ensure the class is always subclassed before use. (2) The class is part of a hierarchy where the abstract keyword signals 'this is not a complete, usable entity on its own.' (3) You use the Template Method pattern with only hook methods (concrete with default no-op). However, if a class has no abstract methods and no reason to be abstract, removing the abstract keyword makes the intent clearer.

items.q: Q6. What is the Template Method Pattern and how does it use abstract classes?
items.a: The Template Method Pattern defines a fixed algorithm skeleton in a concrete method of the abstract class (the 'template method'), while leaving specific steps as abstract methods for subclasses to implement. The template method is often final to prevent subclasses from changing the algorithm structure. Example: DataImporter has a final importData() that calls validate(), readData(), parseData(), and save() in sequence. CSVImporter and JSONImporter implement the abstract steps differently, but the overall algorithm never changes. This is the most natural and widely used design pattern for abstract classes — it embodies 'define the structure, delegate the details.'

items.q: Q7. What happens if a concrete subclass does not implement all abstract methods?
items.a: It causes a COMPILE ERROR: 'ConcreteClass is not abstract and does not override abstract method methodName() in AbstractClass'. The only two valid options when extending an abstract class are: (1) Implement ALL inherited abstract methods in the subclass — making it concrete. (2) Declare the subclass as abstract too — deferring the implementation obligation to further subclasses. There is no runtime consequence because the compiler enforces this before the code runs.

items.q: Q8. Can an abstract class extend another abstract class? Can it extend a concrete class?
items.a: Both are valid. (1) Abstract extends abstract: the extending abstract class does NOT need to implement the parent's abstract methods — it inherits them and passes the obligation to the first concrete subclass. It can add new abstract methods too. (2) Abstract extends concrete: perfectly valid. The concrete parent's methods are inherited. The abstract class may add new abstract methods that its own subclasses must implement. Example: AbstractList (abstract) extends AbstractCollection (abstract) in the JDK.

items.q: Q9. Why should abstract class constructors be protected, not public?
items.a: Abstract class constructors can never be called directly with 'new' — only through super() from subclasses. Making them public is misleading — it suggests they can be called directly, which they cannot. Protected access is the correct and idiomatic choice: it allows subclasses in any package to call super(...), while signaling to all other code that this constructor is not for direct use. A public constructor on an abstract class is not a compile error, but it is a design violation that confuses API readers.

items.q: Q10. What is a concrete class? Can a concrete class be extended?
items.a: A concrete class is any non-abstract class that provides complete implementations for all its methods (including all inherited abstract methods) and can be directly instantiated with 'new'. Yes, concrete classes can be extended — unless they are declared 'final' (which prevents subclassing). Extending a concrete class creates a subclass that inherits all its behavior. If the subclass adds no new abstract methods and implements any it introduces, it too is concrete. Most JDK classes like ArrayList, HashMap, and String (final — cannot extend) are concrete classes.

Design an abstract class 'Discount' with: a shared field 'discountCode', a constructor, an abstract method 'calculateDiscount(double price)', and a concrete method 'applyDiscount(double price)' that prints the final price after calling calculateDiscount(). Then write two concrete subclasses: 'FlatDiscount' (fixed amount off) and 'PercentageDiscount' (percent off).

An abstract method's entire purpose is to be overridden in subclasses — so 'private abstract' is a direct contradiction. Fix: change private to protected or public: 'protected abstract boolean validate(String input);'

items.q: 5. Implement the Template Method Pattern for a 'DatabaseMigration' abstract class with the template method 'migrate()' that: (1) takes a backup, (2) runs migration scripts, (3) validates the result, (4) sends a report. Steps 2 and 3 are abstract; steps 1 and 4 are shared concrete methods.

Output: 'Color: null'
This demonstrates a subtle and dangerous pattern: calling an overridable method from a constructor. When new ColorPrinter() is called: (1) ColorPrinter() calls super() → Printer constructor runs. (2) Printer() calls print() — which is overridden in ColorPrinter. (3) ColorPrinter.print() executes — but at this point ColorPrinter's fields (including 'color') have NOT yet been initialized (the field initializer 'color = "Blue"' runs AFTER super() returns). So color is still null. This is why abstract class constructors should NEVER call abstract (overridable) methods — it leads to partially-initialized object access. Mark such methods final or move the call out of the constructor.

items.q: 7. Choose between abstract class and interface for each scenario: (a) Shape hierarchy with Circle, Rectangle — all shapes have a color field and a shared draw() method. (b) Sortable behavior for Student, Product, Employee. (c) Document processors for PDF, Word, Excel — all share an author field and a validate() step.
items.a:
(a) Abstract class — Shapes share a 'color' field (state) and a concrete draw() method. IS-A relationship (Circle IS-A Shape). Use: abstract class Shape with protected String color, concrete draw(), abstract calculateArea().
(b) Interface — Student, Product, Employee are from completely different hierarchies with no shared state. CAN-DO capability. Use: interface Sortable { int compareTo(Object other); } — or better, implement java.lang.Comparable<T>.
(c) Abstract class — All document processors share an 'author' field (state) and a concrete validate() method. IS-A relationship. Use: abstract class DocumentProcessor with protected String author, concrete validate(), abstract process(). Rule: if there's shared state → abstract class. If it's just a behavioral contract across unrelated types → interface.

items.q: 8. A class extends an abstract class but only implements some of the abstract methods. What must be true about that class? Can it be used to create objects?
items.a: The class MUST itself be declared abstract — otherwise it's a compile error. It cannot be used to create objects directly (new cannot be called on it). It is an 'abstract subclass' — a valid intermediate level in the hierarchy that provides partial implementation. The unimplemented abstract methods are passed down to further subclasses. The first concrete subclass in the chain that implements ALL remaining abstract methods can be instantiated. This pattern is useful for multi-level hierarchies: abstract Employee → abstract PermanentEmployee (implements bonus logic) → concrete SoftwareEngineer (implements salary, designation).

sections.title: Conclusion — Abstract Classes: The Blueprint Architecture of Java OOP

blocks.text: Abstract classes are the architectural backbone of Java class hierarchies. They define what a family of related classes has in common — shared state, shared behavior, and a common contract — while leaving the specifics to concrete subclasses. They are the mechanism through which Java enforces the Open/Closed Principle: open for extension (add new subclasses), closed for modification (the abstract class's structure remains stable).

The difference between beginner and senior Java code is visible in how they use abstract classes. Beginners either avoid them entirely (duplicating logic across classes) or overuse them (creating deep, rigid hierarchies). Senior developers use abstract classes precisely: as partial implementations with a clear contract, leveraging the Template Method Pattern to define stable algorithms with swappable steps, and preferring interfaces when there is no shared state to justify an abstract class.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Abstract Class & Concrete Class

items.q: What is an abstract class in Java?
items.a: An abstract class is a class declared with the 'abstract' keyword that cannot be instantiated directly. It represents an incomplete design — it may contain abstract methods (no body, only a contract subclasses must fulfill) as well as concrete methods (shared implementation). Abstract classes are extended by concrete subclasses that implement all abstract methods. They are used when a group of related classes shares common state and behavior but differs in specific operations.

items.q: What is the difference between abstract class and interface in Java?
items.a: Abstract class can have instance variables (shared state), constructors, and both abstract and concrete methods; supports single inheritance only. Interface has no instance variables (only constants), no constructors, and all methods are implicitly abstract (except Java 8+ default/static methods); supports multiple inheritance. Use abstract class for IS-A relationships with shared state (Vehicle → Car). Use interface for CAN-DO capabilities across unrelated types (Runnable, Serializable).

items.q: Can an abstract class have a constructor in Java?
items.a: Yes. Abstract classes can have constructors. They cannot be called with 'new AbstractClass()' directly, but they are invoked through super() calls in subclass constructors. They initialize the shared fields declared in the abstract class. Abstract class constructors should be protected — they are never called directly, only via the inheritance chain.

items.q: What is an abstract method in Java?
items.a: An abstract method is declared with the 'abstract' keyword and has no body — only a signature and semicolon: 'public abstract void doWork();'. It defines a contract that every concrete subclass must implement. Abstract methods cannot be private, static, or final. They can only exist inside abstract classes or interfaces.

items.q: What is a concrete class in Java?
items.a: A concrete class is any non-abstract class that provides complete implementations for all its methods — including all abstract methods inherited from parent abstract classes or interfaces. It can be directly instantiated with 'new'. Most ordinary Java classes are concrete classes. If a class extends an abstract class but does not implement all abstract methods, it must itself be declared abstract — it cannot be concrete.
